activities.name: ggPoolMatch

config.prompt: Sovereignty re-instrumented — pair each term with its example:

pairs.right: tariff-setting to the WTO, monetary policy to a common central bank
over what unilateral action could no longer deliver
the same decades that raised trade shares multiplied border agencies, capital-scan systems and sanctions regimes

config.why: Globalisation and sovereignty are not opposites — states deliberately pool powers precisely to regain control.

activities.caption: true or false — is the UN a world government?
activities.name: ggUNJudge

statements.why: It is a coordination and legitimation platform for sovereign states — funded by members, not a sovereign.

statements.s: The UN has a standing army.
statements.why: Its 'binding' resolutions require member states to enforce them.

statements.s: It succeeds at technical coordination — vaccines, standards, peacekeeping logistics.
statements.why: That is the platform at work beneath the veto headlines.

statements.s: It fails exactly where enforcement meets a permanent member's veto.
statements.why: Paralysis by design wherever great-power interests clash.

activities.caption: drag the divider — 1945's map versus today's
activities.name: ggPowerCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the power map the institutions encode, then and now:

before.label: 1944–45 design
before.text: The unipolar assumptions built in: five permanent members with vetoes, an IMF weighted vote, the G7 at about two-thirds of world GDP.

after.label: the shifting present
after.text: The G7 falls well under half of world GDP, the G20 is elevated after the 2008 crisis, and an expanded BRICS (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE in 2024) formalises the adjustment.

config.why: The governance system still encodes 1945's power map — and legitimacy is leaking exactly along that discrepancy.

activities.anchor: Compliance is actually high day to day
activities.caption: one line of this international-law briefing is wrong
activities.name: ggLawSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's briefing on international law is wrong — click it:
lines: Day-to-day compliance runs high: mail crosses borders, planes land, tariffs are paid, treaties are reported against.
States care about reputation, reciprocity and domestic ratification costs.
Enforcement is abundant at every level of the power distribution because institutions coerce states routinely.
Keohane's finding: cooperation survives hegemonic decline when institutions lower the cost of trust.
config.correction: Enforcement is scarce at the top of the power distribution; below it, institutions quietly coordinate most interactions most of the time.
config.why: Compliance runs on consent, reputation and incentive rather than coercion — which is why the system keeps working even where no hegemon enforces.

activities.caption: order the rungs of regional integration up to the EU
activities.name: ggEuOrder

config.prompt: The ladder regionalism climbs — assemble it from shallowest to deepest:
items: A single market (1993) with four freedoms — goods, services, capital, people
A regulatory state whose standards propagate worldwide — the Brussels effect
config.why: The EU is the deepest integration ever attempted: 27 states, a parliament, a court with primacy over national law — a novel, contested middle between superstate and treaty club.
